label: Two credentials of the same factor are not MFA

mentor.diagnosis: You counted two things as multifactor when they belong to the same factor category.
contrast: Password plus push notification to an enrolled phone
mentor.rule: Count the categories, not the credentials. Two of the same category is still single factor.
mentor.tell: PIN and security question are both knowledge. They are the exam's favourite fake second factor.
mentor.trap: Two prompts feel like two factors, and the login flow looks identical to real MFA.

label: MAC vs DAC vs RBAC vs ABAC vs rule-based

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on a keyword rather than on who decides access and what the decision is based on.
contrast: The system, centrally, users cannot override
Labels and clearances, classic in government and military
The owner's discretion, classic file share permissions
Attributes combined: department, device, location, time, sensitivity
Conditions applied to everyone, such as a time of day restriction
mentor.rule: Owner decides is DAC. System enforces labels is MAC. Job title is RBAC. Multiple combined conditions is ABAC.
mentor.tell: 'Contractors may access it only from a managed device, during business hours, from inside the country' is ABAC, because it is several attributes at once.
mentor.trap: RBAC covers most real organisations, so it is the comfortable default. If the stem lists conditions beyond job function, it is ABAC.

label: Least privilege vs need to know vs separation of duties

mentor.diagnosis: You applied the wrong principle to the scenario. They limit different things.
contrast: An authorised analyst browsing unrelated case files
One person completing a whole sensitive process
The person who raises the payment also approves it
One person holding a role indefinitely
Fraud that only survives because nobody else does the job
mentor.rule: Least privilege is about permissions, need to know is about data, separation of duties is about splitting a process between people.
mentor.tell: 'The same employee can both create and approve' is separation of duties, every time.
mentor.trap: Least privilege is true of almost every access scenario, so it is always defensible and often not the most precise answer.

label: SSO vs federation, and SAML vs OAuth vs OIDC vs LDAP

mentor.diagnosis: You treated these as four names for logging in once. They answer different questions: SSO and federation describe the arrangement, SAML and OAuth are the protocols that carry it, and LDAP is not in that family at all.
contrast: One login reused across many applications
Trust between separate organisations' identity systems
XML assertions passed between IdP and service provider
Yes, the classic enterprise federation protocol
Delegated access to a resource via tokens
An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0
A protocol for querying a directory of users and groups
Directory access; can authenticate via bind
No, it is an internal directory protocol
mentor.rule: SAML says who you are. OAuth says what this app may do on your behalf. OIDC is OAuth with identity bolted on. LDAP is how you look someone up in the directory, not how you federate.
mentor.tell: A stem naming an identity provider and a service provider, or mentioning assertions, tokens, scopes or a directory query.
mentor.trap: OAuth is the single most common wrong answer to an authentication question. It was designed to grant access to a resource without handing over your password, which is authorisation. If the stem asks how the user proved who they are, OAuth alone is not it.

label: Provisioning, de-provisioning, identity proofing and attestation

mentor.diagnosis: You collapsed the account lifecycle into creating and deleting accounts. The objectives separate four activities because the gaps between them are where standing access accumulates.
contrast: Are you really this person, before an account exists?
Accounts issued to whoever asked convincingly
What access does this role need on day one?
Access copied from a colleague, inheriting their accumulated rights
Does this person still need what they have?
Privilege creep: rights gathered through every role change, never removed
Is every path closed the day they leave?
Dormant accounts, which is how former staff and attackers both get back in
mentor.rule: Proofing comes before the account, provisioning sets it up, attestation periodically re-justifies it, and de-provisioning closes it. Privilege creep is an attestation failure, not a provisioning one.
mentor.tell: A long-serving employee who has moved between departments, or a leaver who still has access.
mentor.trap: Copying an existing user's permissions is fast and is the most common provisioning mistake on the exam. It grants everything that user accumulated, which nobody has reviewed.

label: Which password setting fixes which problem: length, complexity, age, expiration, reuse

mentor.diagnosis: You reached for the setting you have seen most often rather than the one that addresses the attack described. Each lever counters a different thing and several of them counter nothing.
contrast: What it does not help with
Offline cracking and brute force; by far the strongest lever
A password already stolen or phished
Much else; it reliably produces predictable substitutions
Users cycling through passwords to return to a favourite
Limiting how long a compromise stays useful
Current guidance discourages routine rotation: it drives weaker, patterned choices
Returning to a previously used password
Reuse of the same password on other sites
Unique, long, random passwords per site
Nothing, if the vault password is weak and unprotected
mentor.rule: Length beats complexity. Minimum age stops the cycling trick, history stops the return, expiration is the one modern guidance has moved away from.
mentor.tell: A stem describing cracking an offline hash dump, or users rotating straight back to a familiar password.
mentor.trap: Forced expiry feels like diligence and is the answer most people pick. Current NIST guidance says rotate on evidence of compromise, not on a calendar, because routine rotation measurably weakens the passwords chosen.

label: Hard token vs soft token vs security key vs biometric vs passwordless

mentor.diagnosis: You sorted these by how modern they sound rather than by what form the authenticator takes and which attacks it survives.
contrast: Dedicated physical device showing a code
No, the code can be read out and relayed
An app on a general-purpose phone
No, same relay problem, plus the phone's own exposure
Physical key using origin-bound public key crypto
Yes: the signature is bound to the real site's origin
Depends on the implementation; local match is strongest
An approach, not a device: no shared secret at all
A message to a phone number
No, and the number can be ported away from you
mentor.rule: A code you can read and type can be relayed to an attacker. A security key signs a challenge bound to the site's origin, so it cannot be replayed to a lookalike domain. That is the whole phishing-resistance argument.
mentor.tell: A stem about users being tricked into entering a valid code on a convincing fake site.
mentor.trap: Passwordless is not automatically strong and is not a factor. It describes removing the shared secret; the strength comes from whatever authenticator replaces it.

label: Just-in-time permissions vs password vaulting vs ephemeral credentials

mentor.diagnosis: You treated privileged access management as one feature. The objectives name three distinct techniques, and they remove different parts of the standing-access problem.
contrast: Shared admin passwords living in people's heads and spreadsheets
The account is still privileged all the time; checkout is audited
Standing privilege: rights are granted on request, for a window, then revoked
The identity persists; only the elevation is temporary
The durable credential itself: issued per session, expiring in minutes
Little, which is why it is the strongest of the three
The manual process around all of the above
Whatever you did not configure it to cover
mentor.rule: Vaulting controls who can take the key. Just-in-time controls when the lock works at all. Ephemeral credentials mean there is no lasting key to steal.
mentor.tell: A stem about administrators holding permanent elevated rights, or shared accounts whose password everyone knows.
mentor.trap: Vaulting is often presented as solving standing privilege and it does not. The account stays privileged around the clock; you have only controlled distribution of its password.
